summary: AE + SE walk through Redwood structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool-calling. Demo shows schema enforcement, guardrails, and an example payment-authorize function call. Discussed hosted vs dedicated, VPC/private deployment, SOC2/KMS, latency vs cost tradeoffs, and next steps to run a pilot benchmark with customer dataset.
transcript:
Header: 2027-04-22 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (CS), Alex Chen (Nova CTO), Maya Rios (Eng Mgr), Samir Patel (Lead ML), Rina Gomez (Security)

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll run about 40ish minutes, demo of structured output and function calling, then Q&A. Maya, Alex, you good with that agenda?
[00:16] Alex (Nova): Yeah that's perfect, we mainly want to see JSON mode and how you'd guard outputs — we do PCI-adjacent stuff so correctness and auditability is key.
[00:28] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, quick intro — I'll demo the JSON structured-output mode and then show an example of function-calling for payment authorization, and finally a quick tour of Console Optimize recommendations.
[00:40] Maya (Nova): Cool, and timeline-wise, we're looking at a Q3 pilot if things look good.
[00:48] Jordan: Excellent, good to know. Briefly, can you share current stack — inferences served in-house or cloud?
[00:57] Samir (Nova): We're running an internal inference cluster for customer support NLU, but not production payments yet, mostly on mixed GPU fleet — some quantized instances, some float16. Latency is about 200-300ms tail for short prompts, cost is creeping up.
[01:17] Rina (Security): From security side we need SOC2 scope, audit logs, KMS integration, and VPC options for anything touching customer PII.
[01:29] Jordan: Noted — Redwood has hosted, dedicated reserved capacity, and private VPC options; all support KMS and audit logs. We'll show some of that in Console.

--- Demo start ---
[02:10] Priya: Ok starting the demo. First slide shows structured output — this is JSON mode where you declare a schema for the model to fill. The key point is we can validate and coerce fields, run guardrails to ensure types and enumerations, and optionally re-run or call a function when output doesn't match.
[02:40] Priya: Example schema: { transaction_id: string, amount: number, currency: string, authorized: boolean, reason: string? } — so optional reason. I'll paste a sample prompt that asks the model to extract payment intent and call authorize_payment if authorized is true.
[03:03] Alex: One question — how deterministic is the schema enforcement? We need to ensure fields like amount are numbers, not strings or 'ten dollars'.
[03:13] Priya: Good question. The pipeline applies a two-step process: (1) structured-output mode instructs the model to emit JSON strictly, with examples and a format_instructions token; (2) Redwood runs a validator on the result — simple type coercion ("10.00" -> 10.0) and pattern checks, or it flags mismatch and can route to a fallback model or a re-prompt. You can also wire in a function call to do strict parsing server-side.
[03:42] Samir: And if model hallucinated a field, do you have an attest/logging trace for audits?
[03:50] Priya: Yes, audit logs capture input prompt, model output, validation result, and any function calls / webhook responses. Everything can be stored in the Console and exported, and we support customer-managed KMS for encryption-at-rest.

[04:10] Priya: Now I'll demo the function-calling flow. I trigger an example where the model outputs JSON and then Redwood triggers a function authorize_payment(webhook_url, payload). The function-schema is declared in the API — you can map fields to your service.
[04:35] [screen share: code] Priya: Here's the request payload: { transaction_id: "txn_12345", amount: 150.00, currency: "USD", payer: { id: "cust_999" } } — the model decides authorized: true and we call the function.
[04:58] [screen] The webhook mock returns { status: "ok", auth_code: "AUTH-77" } and Redwood attaches that response to the transcript/event.
[05:12] Alex: That attachment — does it show in Console and audit logs?
[05:18] Priya: Yes, Console shows request/response pairs, latency, and any downstream errors. You can redact or mask fields at logging time for PCI scope.

[05:40] Maya: How do you prevent the model from issuing a call for e.g. refunds when it's not allowed? We need guardrails to block certain actions.
[05:51] Priya: Two layers: first, schema-level constraints (enum of allowed actions), second, policy-engine checks in the routing layer: pre- and post-hooks can assert authorization; if mismatch, Redwood can block the call and surface an error instead of executing. We also support RBAC so only certain API keys or roles can trigger live webhooks.
[06:18] Samir: Any rate limiting on function calls?
[06:22] Jordan: Yes, per-route rate limits and quota gating — you can restrict webhook call volume independent of token usage. That helps protect downstream systems.

[06:40] Priya: Switching gears to Console: here is the per-route dashboard — token breakdown, latency distribution, and a new structured-output monitor that tracks schema mismatch rate over time. You can set alerts if mismatch > 1% or if authorized==false spikes.
[07:03] Priya: Also Optimize recommendations — we show batching suggestions, KV cache opportunities for repeated prefixes, and quantization recommendations based on your sequence-length distribution.
[07:18] Alex: For payments, we need strict tail latency SLAs — what's realistic with Redwood hosted vs dedicated?
[07:27] Priya: Hosted: depends on model size and region, but for small chat models you can get 100-200ms typical for short responses; dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable throughput and lower tail latency because you own the GPU pool. For strict SLAs we recommend Dedicated or Private deployment with pinned model variants and prewarmed pools.
[07:49] Maya: What's the minimum commit for dedicated?
[07:52] Jordan: We have a few tiers; I'll send the deck but typical entry is monthly reserved GPUs for a predictable commit — pricing deck will detail.

[08:15] [10-min demo clip collapsed — priya runs example variations showing schema mismatches and auto-reprompt] 
[09:05] Priya: Here's a case where model returned amount as "one fifty" — Redwood's validator flagged mismatch, attempted coercion, failed, and then triggered an automatic re-prompt with clarifying instruction. It resolved in the second pass.
[09:26] Samir: Ok that's useful. For throughput, if we have bursts of authorizations during peak, can Redwood do autoscaling without breaking our downstream rate limits?
[09:38] Jordan: Yes, you can configure burst policies and route to a lower-cost fallback model when capacity is constrained; you can also buffer outbound webhook calls or rate-limit them at the adapter layer to preserve downstream stability.

[10:05] Rina: Quick security: we need SSO for users, audit retention for 1 year, KMS/HSM, and an option to deploy control plane inside our VPC. Does Redwood support that?
[10:16] Jordan: Yes, SSO/SAML and RBAC — retention windows configurable, KMS customer-managed keys supported for Private deployments, and we offer a private control plane option where the management plane runs in your VPC. I'll include details in security pack.

[11:00] Priya: Now a short live run: I'm going to push a prompt that asks for a payment authorization and include a policy that blocks calls above $10k automatically.
[11:18] [screen share: logs] Priya: Model returned authorized true for $150; function called, webhook succeeded, Console shows 120ms function call latency, total end-to-end 310ms — includes network + function.
[11:37] Alex: That 310ms — is that typical? We were hoping to be sub-200ms for authorizations.
[11:43] Priya: The biggest variable is your webhook latency; the Redwood runtime is generally sub-150ms for small responses. If you host the webhook inside same cloud region and use dedicated capacity you'll see lower end-to-end numbers.

[12:05] Luis (CS): We can coordinate a benchmark where Nova hosts a mock webhook in their VPC and we run a 10k transaction replay to measure p95/p99.
[12:15] Maya: That would be ideal.

[12:28] Priya: Quick note on observability: you can trace a request through Console, see model tokens used, CVs, kernel selection, and Optimize suggestions like quantize to int8 for cost savings — but note quantization tradeoffs on ACC for specific tasks, we'll help evaluate.

[13:00] Alex: How do we handle model updates — if you change the model or quantization, how do we avoid regressions?
[13:09] Priya: Rollouts support canary and A/B. We also link evals to prompt sets — if a new model causes a regression on your golden prompt set, the Console will flag it and you can auto-fallback.

[13:38] Samir: For the pilot, we'd like to measure semantic accuracy on fraud signals in addition to latency. Can Redwood integrate our eval harness?
[13:47] Priya: Absolutely; you can upload prompt/eval sets or run via API and we can tie quality regressions to alerts. We'll collaborate on the eval criteria during the pilot scoping.

[14:12] [15–30 min: deeper Q&A, some interruptions and background noise briefly]
[20:05] Alex: One last question on data residency — some of our EU customers demand data stay in EU. Can you guarantee region-specific hosting?
[20:17] Jordan: Yes, we have region routing policies and private deployments in EU regions; we'll include region-specific SLAs in the enterprise agreement.

[22:00] Maya: On billing, how granular is usage attribution per route/team? We need per-team chargeback.
[22:10] Jordan: Console has token-level breakdowns per API key and per-route. You can map API keys to teams and export granular usage for internal billing.

[24:00] Priya: Returning to guardrails — we also support syntactic and semantic checks: e.g., block outputs that mention PII via regexes and optional semantic classifiers that can flag sensitive content.
[24:20] Rina: Good — how are those classifiers trained, and do they see our data?
[24:28] Priya: The classifiers can be Redwood-managed or you can bring-your-own; for BYO we run in your private deployment if needed and they don't leave your environment. For hosted, we support contractual protections and SOC2 controls.

[26:45] Jordan: Ok we should recap next steps. I'll send pricing and dedicated tiers; Priya will drop sample schemas and sandbox creds; Nova will provide a test dataset and webhook endpoint. We'll also schedule the benchmark week of 2027-05-03.

[27:10] Alex: Sounds good. Any blockers from security?
[27:14] Rina: I'll review the security pack once Jordan sends it, but initial requirements look supported. I'll get the compliance doc back by Friday.

[27:30] Maya: Timeline — if the benchmark looks good, can we run a 6–8 week pilot in June?
[27:38] Jordan: Yes that aligns.

[28:00] [small crosstalk]
[29:00] Priya: One demo edge-case: if the model suggests an action outside allowed enums, the system logs it and returns an error object instead of calling the function — this avoids accidental actions.
[29:20] Samir: Good. Also, do you support multiple webhook endpoints per environment for canarying?
[29:28] Priya: Yes — you can map routes to endpoint groups and do canary grading based on success rates.

[30:00] Jordan: Alright folks, final quick Qs?
[30:06] Alex: Licensing and support SLA tiers — high level please.
[30:12] Jordan: We have standard support for hosted, premium for dedicated/private with 24/7 pager and priority response; enterprise includes security reviews and a TAM. I'll include specifics.

[31:00] Maya: Anything else on cost optimization?
[31:05] Priya: Use Optimize's batching rules and prefix caching for repeat prompts, and choose quantization profiles per workload — for NLU tasks that can be brittle, test before wholesale quantization.

[33:00] Jordan: Okay, we'll wrap up — thanks everyone. Recap of next steps in the chat and I'll follow up with the deck and security pack.
[33:15] Alex: Thanks, that was helpful.
[33:20] Maya: Thanks all.
[33:25] Rina: Bye.

End of meeting.

Notes: transcript has minor ASR errors (KV cache sometimes spoken as KV cash, occasional run-on sentences). References to artifacts: pricing deck (link: https://redwood.example/decks/pricing-nova), security pack (link: https://redwood.example/sec/sec-pack), sandbox invite (link: https://redwood.example/sandbox/nova).
